Row.Text: Amongst a packed house, Dr Rizal enjoys a comedy from the gallery of an English theatre. Down on stage, a scene of mistaken identity sends waves of laughter through the crowd.
An unquestionably English style of humor.

The earth trembles beneath the cavalry charge, and the yeomen grip their longbows. As one they draw and fire a lethal volley. For a moment, the whir of arrows drowns out the screaming horses and baying trumpets. Then the arrows find their marks with a thousand vicious thuds.
The age of the knight is over.
The French will always fall before England.

In a small study off a crowded street, an astrologer listens intently as a patient recounts recent misfortunes she has suffered. Could she have a secret enemy who has cursed her from afar? Taking her hand, the astrologer reassures her that the heavens always have the answers. Then he turns to consult the stars and planets.
One must always trust the sky.
Does this man have a license to practice?

At England's borders, reivers prey upon the weak and unprepared. Brandishing lang spears, they seize livestock and blackmail locals to fill their larders, hanging all who oppose them and singing ballads of their raids.
This is the brutal law of the borderlands.

Generations of the English devout have never read sacred scripture themselves. Uneducated in the liturgical language, they experience the text through the interpretation of priests. Recently, vernacular translations have begun to spread, allowing all to read and interpret the divine word on their own.
Spiritual growth is an individual endeavor.
A flock needs a shepherd to thrive.

Scribes disseminate the autobiography of a woman who claims close ties with religious figures of old. Between eyewitness accounts of events in the distant past, she challenges the status quo of English communal life, encouraging readers to abandon material pursuits in favor of their spiritual journeys.

Powerful lords protest the growing influence of one noble family, possessing many titles and a voice that seems to drown all others at court. Scorning attempts at peace, the united houses demand the exile of their foes – or else.
This is a monarchy, not an oligarchy.
Free Promotion on highest Level Commander, but {1_reward} in all Settlements.
The exile of one family is a small price for peace.

Thousands flock to the Globe Theatre to see performances penned by a famous playwright. They explore contemporary issues through tales of the past, some comedic, some tragic, all thrilling for peasants and aristocrats alike.
The English see themselves reflected on stage.
What exciting stories to pass an afternoon.

As England's eyes drift to lands beyond its borders, the Board of Trade fields questions on how to handle these new settlements. Many agree that colonies should repay their founding investments through commodities. But concern lingers that local cultures may influence them away from English lifestyles.
A colony's purpose is to enrich the core.
England shall learn from the world.
These colonies might someday take on a life of their own...

On a well-traveled road through an ancient forest, an outlaw and his band of merry men seize goods from passing travelers. They say they take from the rich to give to the poor, sparking the local sheriff's ire but fueling peasant support of their thefts.
These pests will be dealt with.

Historians at Oxford comb through an expansive set of casebooks written by an astrologer several centuries ago. Amid records of patient visits and astrological readings sits a booklet of opinions about plays by a famous playwright of his age.
They offer valuable contemporary insight into these works.
His opinions are as suspect as his medical skills.

A new printing phenomenon has struck England - “Travailles of the Grete Marchauntes,” richly-illustrated but mass-printed profiles of merchant adventurers and their increasingly unrealistic adventures. Charter companies worry that these create unrealistic expectations… but they do sell.
Next installment: “The Case of the Fifty Thousand Venomous Apes”.
Next installment: “Charles and the Compound Interest”.
Stone-hall and wolf-break, book-hoards and cattle-den - these are the kennings given to the first English towns. The English singers turn cities of mud and smoke into poetry.
So long as they don’t distract the real work of trade.
